$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6\end{aligned}],\,x(t)={e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -10\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the initial value problem and its solution given above. What is the tangent vector to the solution curve at the point corresponding to $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡2?$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that the $xy$-coordinate plane is called the *phase plane* of the system. A particular solution of an initial value problem is called a *trajectory* (or *orbit*).

First, we compute the point that corresponds to $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡2$ on the given trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & ={e}^{(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+{e}^{-2(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -10\end{aligned}] \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{59}{4} \\ \frac{11}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the equation of our system, we obtain the tangent vector to the trajectory.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{59}{4} \\ \frac{11}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2(\frac{59}{4})-2(\frac{11}{2}) \\ 2(\frac{59}{4})-3(\frac{11}{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{37}{2} \\ 13\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6\end{aligned}],\,x(t)={e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -10\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the initial value problem and its solution given above. What is the tangent vector to the solution curve at the point corresponding to $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡2?$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that the $xy$-coordinate plane is called the *phase plane* of the system. A particular solution of an initial value problem is called a *trajectory* (or *orbit*).

First, we compute the point that corresponds to $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡2$ on the given trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & ={e}^{(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+{e}^{-2(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -10\end{aligned}] \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{59}{4} \\ \frac{11}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the equation of our system, we obtain the tangent vector to the trajectory.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{59}{4} \\ \frac{11}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2(\frac{59}{4})-2(\frac{11}{2}) \\ 2(\frac{59}{4})-3(\frac{11}{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{37}{2} \\ 13\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t)-2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. Find equations of the $x$- and $y$-nullclines for the corresponding phase space.$\,$
The $x$-nullcline is $y=$ {{field-1}}. 

$\,$
The $y$-nullcline is $y=$ {{field-2}}.
after.worked_solution:
Recall that: 

- The $x$-nullcline is a line for which ${x}^{′}=0$ (i.e., the tangents to trajectories are vertical). So, to find it, we set the first equation of the system equal to $0:$

$$
2x-2y=0\,⇒\,y=x
$$

- The $y$-nullcline is a line for which ${y}^{′}=0$ (i.e., the tangents to trajectories are horizontal). So, to find it, we set the second equation of the system equal to $0:$

$$
2x+3y=0\,⇒\,y=-\frac{2}{3}x
$$

after.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,x(t)={e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the initial value problem and its solution given above. What is the tangent vector to the solution curve at the point corresponding to $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡3?$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that the $xy$-coordinate plane is called the *phase plane* of the system. A particular solution of an initial value problem is called a *trajectory* (or *orbit*).

First, we compute the point that corresponds to $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ on the given trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\operatorname{ln}⁡3) & ={e}^{2(\operatorname{ln}⁡3)}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =9[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 9\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the equation of our system, we obtain the tangent vector to the trajectory.

$$
